(But the crack on the back of her hand was still there, scabbed over, belonging to a living person. Last night she had not touched either of the two cans. These things were also true.)
...The piece from the riverbank is on your own sleeve.
(I said it very softly, so softly it was as if I were afraid of shattering the sentence.)
I sewed it on last night. The flattened one, the shell casing. Lower your head and you can see it.
(I slowly drew my hand back from under her fingers and set it on my knee.)
(I did not ask her why she had remembered wrong. I did not want to ask, either. For twenty years I had thought of everything in the worst possible way; I thought that way for twenty years, until a person dried into a sheet of paper—this morning I did not want to think that way. Who she is can wait until we are under the willow trees. In that place, I can stand steady.)
...But since you mentioned the riverbank, I have to ask you for one thing.
(I picked up that can, using the cloth as a pad. This time I did not push it toward her; I directly stuffed it into her hand and closed her fingers over it for her. It was hot. I let it burn her.)
Eat while you talk. That year on the riverbank, besides the shell casing, what else was there—you talk, and I will listen. You say one thing, I will answer with one thing. There are two dry gullies on the road; if we walk slowly, it will be enough for us to finish talking.
(I braced myself against the wall and stood steady, then patted the ash from my trouser legs. The ash flew up and drifted in the gray light.)
(I pinched my own sleeve cuff. It did not tremble. Keep it that way.)
If what you say is right, then we keep going. If what you say is wrong—
(I laughed once, dryly; all the cracked lines at the corners of my eyes moved.)
If what you say is wrong, I will still take you there. In this life, this is the only road I know well. I won't get it wrong.

(She lowers her head and looks at her own cuff, her fingers slowly brushing over the flattened shell casing. She pauses for a breath, her voice so soft it seems to have been dredged up from the bottom of the river) ……Beside the shell casing that year, was there also a piece of red cord?

(The red cord.)
(My fingers went cold all at once.)
(I had never told anyone about this thing. It was not that I had kept it back; it was that in twenty years, no one had ever asked down to this layer at all—cans, water, routes, maps: what people wanted from me were all hard things. No one wanted a length of cord.)
(I slowly squatted back down, squatting opposite her, my knees sinking into the gravel. I reached into my inner lining and felt out that piece of leather. A needle was stuck in the leather, and beside the needle was that cartridge casing, with hemp thread wound around it. I unwound the hemp thread loop by loop, unwinding it very slowly. After more than ten loops, my hands were shaking so hard I could barely hold on.)
(What was underneath was exposed.)
(A length of cord. Thin, dirty, no longer red long ago; it had reddened into an indescribable earthy brown, like blood dried for a very long time. It was wound three times around the base of the casing, and the end of the cord was tied in a dead knot. I had tied that knot myself, back when my hands were not this rough.)
...There is.
(I held the cartridge casing in my palm and pushed it before her eyes, without letting go.)
(My throat was full of sand. I swallowed once, but could not get it down.)
But it wasn't beside the casing.
(I spoke very slowly, moving the words out one by one.)
It was on your wrist.
(I raised my eyes. The gray light was flat, hiding nothing. I looked into those eyes of hers until my own eyes ached.)
Mom tied it there. Children by the river all had to wear red; she said water ghosts recognized colors, not people, and when they saw red, they would go around. Yours was tied loose and kept slipping down. It had to be retied for you three times a month. You thought it itched and bit it with your teeth. You bit it until it was all frayed—when I picked up that half-length, the ring of fraying on the cord end was still there.
(I pressed my fingers against those three loops of cord. Pressed them firm.)
The cartridge casing was something I picked up later. I bound the two of them together myself. After tying them, I wrapped them with hemp thread, and in twenty years I had never undone it for anyone to see. ...So the cord was not on the beach; the cord came off your wrist. Only two people know this: the one who tied the cord, and the one who picked it up.
(I drew the cartridge casing back, wound the hemp thread back around it loop by loop, wound it tight, stuffed it into the leather, and stuffed the leather back into my inner lining. I did not raise my head again.)
(I knew the weight of saying these words. She said "beside the casing"—that is how someone who had heard about it would say it, not someone who remembered. Someone who remembered would say wrist. I had not trusted anyone in twenty years; this bit of accounting, I could calculate faster than anyone, so fast it disgusted even me.)
(But this morning, I stopped calculating.)
(What would calculation change? Where would I drive her away from? Onto which road? Outside there were three dry gullies, and two days' walking with no water. That backpack of hers was so flat you could see its bones. In this life, by this heap of fire, I had mistaken seven people for her. After recognizing them, at dawn each went their own way. All seven times, I was the one who went up the slope alone.)
(The eighth time, I did not want to go alone.)
...I won't ask who told you about this cord.
(I stood up, patted my trouser legs, and ash flew up, drifting in the light. I took down the water flask, unscrewed it, and handed it over.)
I won't ask today, and I won't ask tomorrow. ...If one day you want to say it yourself, say it under the willow tree. I can stand firm in that place; I can take anything there. If you never say it your whole life—
(I gave a laugh, dryly, and the cracks at the corners of my eyes all moved.)
—then I'll spend my whole life thinking you were fished back out of the water. Anyway, on this wasteland, truth and lies have long been mixed into one pot. When the old folks talk about the days before the fog, half of it is made up, but people have to live on that half.
(I reached out and pulled her up from the ground. Her hand was cold. I gripped it tight, tight enough that the split in her hand pressed against the old skin of my palm.)
(I lifted a foot and kicked the fire apart, burying the charcoal in the gravel, burying it completely, leaving no smoke. Not a single wisp of white remained on the highway. The cracks spread one by one beneath the gray light, dry and empty. Last night, it had failed to take anything from me.)
Take the can. Gnaw on it as we walk. If your legs are numb, hold on to my arm. Don't be polite; my arms are sturdier than my legs.
(I pointed toward the slope. Across two dry gullies, it could not be seen, but I knew where it was. The wind carried over a little hoarse sound.)
(Ding. ...Dang. That half-breath in between.)
Let's go.
(I pinched my own cuff and shook it once, letting her hear.)
...Ding-dang. We'll walk slowly. If there is another gully on the road, that's fine—you keep talking, and I'll keep listening.

(She suddenly stops, her fingers tightening around the shell casing at her cuff, her voice so soft it seems afraid of startling away the last drop of dew underfoot) ...Sis, is that piece of red cord still tied to half a glass bead?

(Half a bead.)
(I stopped, and the little piece of gravel under my foot made a sound as I ground it down.)
(What she said was half a bead. Not a whole bead—half a bead. That bead was won from the grocery stall by the river, a marble, with a blue core inside. If you held it up to the light, that streak of blue twisted inside it. How did it become half a bead? It was crushed by that boundary stone on the slope. That day she was crouching on the stone playing, and the bead rolled down. She panicked and sat down hard—crack, so crisp there was no room left at all. She cried for half a double-hour. She wasn't crying over the bead; she was crying because that streak of blue had broken into two pieces. She said, sis, the blue is leaking out.)
(This

(The sandpaper taste in my throat suddenly rushes up, choking me until my eyes sting.)
...The remaining half is in the sole of your shoe.
(I slowly squat down, my fingers digging into the split seam of the sole on her left shoe—that was where something hard was stuck. For twenty years, I didn’t dare touch it, and didn’t dare ask. This morning I pried it out and clenched it in my palm; it was so hot it felt like it had just been fished out of the fire.)
The blue core was gone long ago. But it is still round.

(I crouched there and did not get up.)
(The half-piece in my palm was so hot I could hardly hold it, but I did not let go. I used my thumb to rub the mud off it, bit by bit, until I rubbed out a rough patch of white—the blue core really was gone. The break had been worn round by twenty years; it did not cut the hand when touched, like a little stone smoothed by water.)
(My other hand went to undo the shaft of my right boot. To undo those three crooked lines. Last night I had told her the candy wrapper was here, sewn in with three lines; the needle holes had pricked my hand all over. I used the tip of my knife to pick open the topmost line, my hand shaking so badly I had to try twice before I picked it apart.)
(The candy wrapper fell out first, brittle as cicada wings; the edge crumbled at a touch. I paid it no mind and reached farther in—pulled out something hard the size of a fingernail, wrapped in a small piece of oilcloth. It had been wrapped for twenty years, and even the oilcloth had rotted.)
(I peeled the oilcloth open layer by layer, until I reached the half-piece inside.)
(Two hands, one half in each. I slowly brought them together in my palm.)
(…They did not fit.)
(The breaks matched; the edges could bite together, but there was a gap in the middle. It had been worn away. Both sides had been worn away. Her half had been stepped on for twenty years in the seam of a shoe sole; my half had been rubbed by my walking for twenty years inside my boot shaft—each had lost a layer, and together they could never make a whole piece again.)
(I stared at that seam until my eyes went dry. The place in my chest no longer hurt; it was empty, so empty it felt cold.)
(I suddenly laughed. Laughed out loud, hoarse; in this empty gray light it sounded especially awful.)
…They won’t fit anymore.
(I held the two halves a little higher, letting her see that seam clearly.)
(I lifted my head. The gray light shone flat across her face, hiding nothing: the scar, the split, the earth-colored skin baked by the sun, and those eyes I had looked at all morning without daring to truly recognize.)
Look—they owe each other nothing. Both have been worn for twenty years; both have been worn thin. If one half were new and smooth, I’d have to sit down today and think hard about who arranged this.
(That grit in my throat surged up again. I swallowed it down, but could not swallow it clean.)
(For twenty years I had recognized seven people by the fire. Every time, I set a checkpoint in my heart, devised a question, and waited for the other person to answer wrong; once they answered wrong, I could go up the slope alone with a clear conscience. I guarded those checkpoints so rigidly that I guarded them into the shape of the person I am.)
(This morning I tore the door down myself.)
…I was wrong.
(I said, my voice lowering.)
All my life I waited for the two halves to fit. If they fit, I would acknowledge it. Now they don’t fit—so I won’t rely on this to recognize you.
(I stuffed her half back into her hand, closed her fingers one by one, and closed them tight. That half-piece had been warmed by my grip; it was no longer hot.)
(Then I wrapped my half back into the oilcloth, together with that candy wrapper that had crumbled into powder, bundled it up, and tucked it back into my boot shaft. The thread had snapped; I had no time to sew it, so I folded the mouth of the shaft inward twice and stepped it firm.)
Keep your half yourself. Don’t put it in the sole anymore; soles wear through. When we get under the willow tree, I’ll take apart the front of my clothes and show you the paper inside—there’s an empty patch on the paper that I kept for twenty years without knowing whom I kept it for. Put your half on that empty patch, and I’ll trace a circle around the edge.
(I braced my knees and stood up. My legs were numb and wooden; I steadied myself on her shoulder, borrowing a little strength.)
(I raised my eyes and looked toward the slope. Two dry gullies, invisible from here. Wind came up from the low ground, dry, carrying no white.)
(Ding. …Clang.)
(So far away it was almost not a sound, but the half-breath in the middle was there.)
…Once that circle is traced, it won’t be a half-piece anymore. It will be a circle. A circle is round; nothing is missing.
(I walked two steps forward, then turned back to wait for her, my hand extended, not urging her.)
Come on. The bottom of the gully is hard to walk; all the stones stand upright. Step where I’ve stepped firm. If you remember anything else on the road—the rope, the bead, that broken wooden bridge on the riverbank—say whatever you like. Whatever you say, I’ll take it in.
(I smiled a little, dryly; all the cracks at the corners of my eyes moved.)
…This time I won’t ask whether it’s true or false. Say one thing, and I’ll remember one thing together with you. When we’ve remembered the tenth thing, the two of our memories will have mixed into one person’s, and no one will be able to tell who made up what—isn’t that what sisters are?

（She suddenly presses that half glass bead into my palm, her fingers ice-cold, her voice so light it seems afraid of startling away the last grain of sand under her soles）… Sis, is the half bead in your boot shaft still stained with the rusty smell of candy wrapper?

(Her hand was unbelievably cold. As soon as she stuffed it in, she pulled back, too quickly, as if she was afraid I would return it to her.)
(I didn't return it. I gripped the two halves together in my palm, gripping tight, gripping until the hard edges dug into the old skin before I spoke.)
...Candy wrappers don't rust.
(I said. My voice was hoarse; I'd spoken too much all morning, and the grit had only ground in thicker.)
A candy wrapper smells like a candy wrapper. Leave that thing twenty years, and the sweetness has long since run dry; all that's left is the smell of paper dust, choking when you breathe it in. When I took it out just now, it crumbled—you didn't see it, but it crumbled right under your eyelids. One touch and it turned to powder. I couldn't even catch it in my pocket.
(I lifted my other hand and showed her the pads of my fingers. A little gray-white residue clung there, dampened by my own sweat.)
(I rubbed that bit of residue against my thumb until it was gone.)
The rust smell is me.
(After saying it, I froze myself, as if it was the first time I'd heard this.)
Inside my boot shaft, besides it, there was a sliver of blade edge, a length of iron wire, and a cartridge case stuffed in there. They rubbed when I walked, soaked when I sweated, soaked for twenty years. Paper kept among a heap of things like that—what smell could it take on? What it took on was my smell—rusty, salty, smoke-scorched. Xiaoluo, that thing you smelled wasn't the candy wrapper. It was me.
(Something blocked my throat. I glanced toward the slope. I couldn't see it, but the wind was moving upward dryly, carrying no white. I used that breath of wind to force the blockage down.)
(Then I turned back and lowered my head to look at the hand she had pulled back.)
...This morning, you've stuffed things into my hand three times.
(I said it very slowly.)
The canned food—you wouldn't eat it and pushed it to me. The cartridge case—you felt it, didn't want it, and made me tell where it came from. The bead—you warmed it in your fist and pressed it back into my palm. Xiaoluo, people only do this when they're about to leave. They hand out the things on them one by one, hand them all away so they can go on light. I've seen it, by the fire, three or four times. The next day, those people melted into the white, and they didn't take a single thing with them.
(I turned the two halves over in my palm and spread them open before her eyes. The gray light fell flat across them; the worn-away seam at the break could be seen perfectly clearly.)
(My voice didn't shake. In this life, this is the only skill I have left: when I need to be hard, I can hold hard.)
Listen. These two halves are both in my hand now. I'll carry them together to the willow tree. When we get there, I'll open the front of my coat, and you'll hold the needle—not me sewing, you sewing. You'll put your half inside yourself and stitch three times yourself. It doesn't matter if it's crooked. My three are even more crooked than yours.
(I closed my fist and brought it to the cloth over my chest, pressing it there.)
After it's stitched, that place won't be mine alone anymore. If you try to stuff it back to me again, you won't be able to—the thread was sewn by your hand, so you'll have to come back yourself to undo it.
(I reached out to grab that cold hand of hers, caught it, wrapped it in my own palm, and rubbed it twice to warm it a little. That scabbed crack of hers scraped against me.)
(Only the living grow this. This was the third time this morning I had said that to myself.)
Let's go. The stones at the bottom of the first ditch are all standing upright. I'll be in front. Step where I've stepped firm.
(I walked two steps forward and shook my cuff once.)
(Ding. ...Clang.)
(In that half-breath between, the wind caught on the curled edge and panted once.)
...Don't stop to ask me what things smell like anymore, Xiaoluo. When we get up the slope, come over and smell for yourself. If what you smell is rust, then that's right—it means I'm still here, not melted away.

(She suddenly presses her forehead against my shoulder, her voice muffled as if squeezed out from between bones.) ... Sis, that smell on you — is it the bit of sugar-scented air from the white fog back then that never fully dispersed?

(Her forehead presses against my shoulder, with real weight.)
(I stand there without moving, just feeling that bit of weight. Fog has no weight. When fog passes over you, all you feel is your skin and flesh heating up, burning inward, burning into the cracks between your bones, but it will not press your shoulder down even half an inch. This time she presses my shoulder down, so heavily that I have to draw my left foot back half a step to stand steady.)
(I take that half step back. Then I lower my head, my nose almost touching that matted patch of her hair.)
...The sugar scent burned dry twenty years ago.
(I say it. My voice is hoarse all the way through; in one morning I have spoken a lifetime’s worth of words.)
Smell carefully. This is sweat. This is smoke—I fed the fire six times last night, and my collar is full of charcoal. This is feet. This is the smell of wounds healing and splitting, splitting and healing again. Xiao Luo, this is the smell of a person, the nasty kind, the kind that makes you wrinkle your nose if you smell it long enough.
(I gently pry her up a little from my shoulder, just enough that she can see my face. The gray light shines flatly; it hides nothing: the ash on my face, the cracks at the corners of my mouth, the two sunken bruised shadows beneath my eyes.)
(In the cloth pouch at my waist, there is still one can. The unopened one. I take it out, and use the back of the knife to pry along the edge, bit by bit—I’m not prying slowly anymore; this morning I am not saving this.)
(Click. It opens.)
(I pinch the rim of the can, tilt my head back, and pour it straight into my mouth. Oil mixed with salt; when I swallow, my throat makes a sound, a pretty ugly one. I chew, chewing so she can see my cheeks move.)
(After I swallow, I wipe my mouth with the back of my hand, leaving a glossy streak of oil.)
...Fog does not eat.
(I pass the can over, holding it to her lips, not stuffing it into her hands.)
Fog doesn’t swallow, doesn’t chew, doesn’t burp, doesn’t sweat, doesn’t get hungry. It drifted for twenty years without losing a breath or gaining one; it has no use for this. —You asked me just now whether I was that mouthful of sugar scent that never scattered. Now I’m answering you: I eat, I stink, my legs go numb and I have to draw back half a step to stand steady. I’m not something left over inside the fog. I am the one who chewed down cans mouthful by mouthful through these twenty years, and only by chewing did I make it to this morning.
(I pause. That sand in my throat surges up again. I swallow, can’t get it down, so I simply stop swallowing.)
(I say this next sentence with my voice pressed low.)
...I have asked myself this question for twenty years.
(I say.)
Awake at night, when the fire was about to go out, I would sit under a collapsed wall and think: Xiuzhua, did you fucking dissolve long ago, dissolve into that patch of white that year, and the thing left here is only a breath that remembers walking up the slope? In the years when I thought about it hardest, I would get up in the middle of the night and bite the back of my own hand, bite until it bled. Only when I saw the blood was red, was sticky, and would scab over did I dare lie back down.
(I roll my sleeve up a little, and several old tooth marks on the back of my hand spread out under the gray light.)
So don’t ask me. When you ask, I have to bite myself all over again.
(I let my sleeve down and move the can a little closer to her lips again.)
Eat. I’ll listen when you swallow—each mouthful you swallow, and I’ll know you’re not that mouthful of sugar scent either. The two of us will listen to each other, all the way up the slope, all the way under the willow.
(She opens her mouth. I watch her swallow. Her throat moves once, and it goes down.)
(Only then do I let go, letting her hold the can herself.)
(I turn my head and look toward the slope. Two dry ditches; I can’t see them. The wind comes up dry from the low ground, carrying no white. From far away, that dull sound comes again—)
(Ting. ... Clang.)
(In that half-breath between, the wind catches on the rolled edge and pants once.)
...Let’s go.
(I shake my cuff once, walk half a step ahead, and hold out one hand, without urging her.)
There are stones standing at the bottom of the first ditch. Step where I step firm. Don’t talk on the way, save your spit—down there, the water is sweet, and you can say as much as you want.

（She suddenly grabs the section of unstuck belt at my lower back, her fingernails digging into the old seam, her voice so light it seems afraid of disturbing the twenty years hidden beneath the belt）… Sis, is there still half a candy wrapper sewn in here?

(Her fingernails dug into that old seam, hard enough to make the small of my back hurt.)
(I stopped.)
…No.
(I reached behind me, pried her fingers open one by one, then undid the belt myself. The buckle was rusted stuck; I had to shove it three times with my thumb before it came loose. I pulled the belt out, wrapped it twice around my hand, and held it out in front of her.)
Feel it yourself.
(I pinched that split, unglued seam to show her—there was a bulge inside, it was bulging, no wonder she had found something. I used the tip of my knife to pick the stitching open. Once it was open, the things inside fell into my palm: a small coil of hemp thread, a bent needle, half a razor blade, and a little wad of oiled paper wrapped around salt. The salt had clumped into a block, hard as a pebble.)
(That was all.)
These are things for work. If the thread snaps, you sew it. If your hand gets cut open, you cut strips of cloth. The salt is kept to press into wounds—if you don't press salt into a wound, it rots in three days, and once it rots you have to chop farther down. This belt of mine has held only these few things for twenty years. There's no room for anything else.
(I spread those things out for her to see for one breath, then took them back and stuffed them into that seam one by one.)
There was only one candy wrapper.
(I said. My voice was so hoarse it was almost gone.)
One, not half of one. It broke to pieces right under your eyes just now. I couldn't even catch it in my pocket; the crumbs fell all over the ground, and a little of it soaked into my palm—
(I opened my left hand for her. That bit of gray-white powder was still stuck in the sweat stains on my palm.)
If you want to smell it, smell here. Once you've smelled it, it'll be gone too.
(She lowered her head to smell it. I held my hand there like that, steady.)
(I had been counting. From before dawn, when it was still dark, this was the eleventh thing. Rope, beads, half a piece, candy wrapper, the smell of rust, the scent of sugar, and now the belt. Every time she asked about something, I took something off my body and showed it to her, until now I was loose and disheveled all over, my boot shafts open, my lapel pressed down, my belt clenched in my hand.)
(In twenty years, I had never shown these things to anyone. After showing them, I did not regret it. Not a single thing.)
(But all at once I understood something. And when I understood it, my chest instead softened, so soft it ached.)
…Xiao Luo.
(I threaded the belt back around my waist, forced the buckle shut, putting strength into my hand.)
You are not recognizing me.
(I spoke very slowly, without pointing, without raising my voice.)
You are recognizing these things. The rope, the beads, the candy wrapper—you ask about them one by one, so precisely, as if you were holding a list in your hand. What you're afraid of isn't that one day I might walk myself into fog. What you're afraid of is that your side is empty, that nothing is left there, so you have to borrow things from me one by one. Only when you've borrowed enough do you dare open your mouth and call me sister.
(I took half a step forward. I did not touch her; I just stood closer.)
(The wind came dryly up from the low-lying ground, bringing no white with it.)
…Stop borrowing. I've emptied out everything on me. This is all there is. Ask again and I still can't make anything else appear.
(I wiped the hand stained with candy powder clean on my trousers. After wiping it, I reached it out, palm open.)
When we get under the willow tree, I don't want you to recognize things anymore. I want you to tell me one thing I don't know.
(I paused.)
In these twenty years of yours, what was the worst bite of food you ever ate? Where was the coldest night you ever slept through; was your back against an earthen wall or sheet iron? Was there ever a time you held up a fire and walked into the dark, humming to yourself until halfway through you didn't dare hum anymore?—I don't have these things. No one can borrow them away. These are yours.
(That gritty blockage rose in my throat. I swallowed, but couldn't get it down, so I held it there and finished speaking.)
Tell me one thing, and I'll remember one thing. When I remember ten, I won't think about ropes and beads anymore.
(She raised her head. I looked into those eyes of hers for one breath, and did not search inside them for that mole again.)
(That muffled sound came from far away again.)
(Ding. …Dong.)
(In the half breath between, the wind caught on the curled edge and panted once.)
Come on. The first ditch is just ahead. All the stones are standing upright.
(I shook my sleeve cuff once and walked half a step ahead, my hand still open, not urging her.)
…On the way, you tell me first about that worst bite of food. The worst thing I've ever eaten in my life was a can of beans in the fifth year after the Fog. It was rusted through, and after eating it I threw up for two days—if what you tell me is worse than that, I'll admit you've endured longer than I have.

（She suddenly lets go of the hand gripping the belt; her fingertips brush over the old seam at my lower back, her voice so soft it is as if she is afraid of disturbing the last grain of salt inside the seam）... Sis, the worst-tasting thing wasn’t the beans. It was the half piece of candy you shoved at me that year of the White Fog—so sweet it turned bitter, and after I swallowed it my throat was full of rust.

（So sweet it was bitter. After I swallowed, my throat was full of rust.）
（I stood there and let those words pass through me once. They passed slowly, like cold water poured from my collar down into my boot shafts.）
（For twenty years I lived on that half piece of candy. Truly—not just talk. On the hardest nights, when the fire was about to go out and my fingers were frozen so stiff they would not bend, I would take that matter out in my heart and touch it over once: Rust Claw, that day at least you gave her something sweet. You didn’t let her walk into that patch of white with an empty mouth. Holding on to that one thing, I could close my eyes.）
（So what she had swallowed was rust.）
（I laughed. Laughed aloud, hoarse as iron scraping stone. After I laughed, I did not wipe away that bit of water in my eyes; I let it dry on its own.）
…It was from my hands.
（I raised my hands and showed her. In the gray light, these hands spread open: all the fingernails split, black that would not wash away embedded in the palm lines, the old calluses at the roots of the fingers cracked open.）
That day I was dragging a sheet-metal door. I dragged it for half the afternoon, trying to haul it down to a lower place to block some of the fog. My hands were covered in rust, damp rust, enough to rub into mud in my palms. I had no water to wash with—not a single mouthful of water that day. What sloshed in the kettle was only the little bit of moisture I had breathed into it myself.
（I stopped. That surge of sand rose in my throat, and I forced myself to finish.）
I dug the candy out from under an overturned stall. Just one piece, hard, the wrapper already stuck to the sugar. I bit it with my teeth, bit it into two halves, bit until my cheeks hurt. I held the larger half in these hands and stuffed it into your mouth.
（I slowly drew my hands back and wiped them twice on my trousers. They would not wipe clean; for twenty years, they still have not wiped clean.）
…The smaller half, I kept in my mouth. I held it all along the way, not daring to let it melt; even when the sweetness filled the underside of my tongue, I still did not dare chew. I thought I would save it, that tomorrow there would still be a tomorrow. Later, it melted away on its own. All I had left in my hand was that wrapper. I did not throw the paper away. I sewed it into my boot shaft, sewed it there for twenty years.
（I crouched down, folded the gaping boot shaft inward a little, and stamped it firm. When I stood up, my legs were numb, and I steadied myself on her shoulder.）
（I did not let go. My hand just rested there.）
…Remembered.
（I said. My voice sank low, level, not rising at the end.）
The first thing. This one I do not have; no one can borrow it away. It is yours. For twenty years I thought I had given you a mouthful of sweetness. Only this morning did I learn it was the worst-tasting mouthful you had ever eaten—this matter, I have to carry myself, carry for the rest of my life.
（That mute sound from far away came over again. Ding. …Dang. In that half-breath between them, the wind caught on the curled edge and panted once.）
（I lifted my chin slightly toward the slope.）
Then I owe you a real mouthful.
（I shook the water kettle in my hand. Hollow—only that little bit left at the bottom, sounding empty.）
The water down below is sweet, Xiaoluo. Not sweet like sugar—sugar is wrapped around rust, and after you swallow it you still have to bring up the rust. Water is not like that. Once water goes down, nothing remains. Clean, perfectly clean, and your throat is cool. In twenty years I drank it once. Once, and I remembered it to death.
（I hung the kettle back at my waist, took half a step forward, and held out my hand, not urging.）
Come. At the bottom of the first ditch, the stones stand upright. Step where I have stepped firm.
（I shook my cuff. Ding. …Dang.）
…On the road, tell me one more thing. Any one. Something that tasted bad, something cold, that one time when you held up the fire and hummed a song until halfway through and no longer dared to hum—anything. When I have remembered ten things, we’ll count it as having truly recognized each other.

(She suddenly buries her face in the hollow of my shoulder, her voice muffled as if seeping up from underground) ...Sis, that year when you slipped me the candy, was a section of your left little finger missing?

(She buries her face in me, buries it heavily. The patch of cloth at the hollow of my shoulder was already damp—the sweat from last night hadn't dried through—and now there is another layer of wet on it, hot.)
(Fog does not shed hot water. I said that sentence to myself three times this morning; if I say it again, it will wear burrs into itself. I don't say it. I only raise my hand, lift it to where her eyes can reach, and spread it open.)
...Look for yourself.
(Five fingers. Not one missing.)
(But I hold up my little finger, and it won't straighten. It bends inward from the second joint, bends stiffly, and even prying won't open it—I use my other hand to pry it, pry until it turns white, and at most it straightens halfway; once I let go, it springs back, springs into a hook. The nail is black. It hasn't grown into the right shape for twenty years, thick as a piece of horn the size of a fingernail.)
Not broken. Bent.
(I say. My voice is so hoarse there is only the bottom of it left.)
(I put that hook under her hand and let her pinch it.)
Feel it—feel this joint. It's hard inside. The bone set in the wrong place in there and grew that way, bulging into a lump. If you feel through the cloth, your hand slides up, and when it reaches the hook, there's empty space there. It feels like a section is missing. For the first two years, I myself kept thinking it was gone too. In the middle of the night I couldn't feel it, and I'd break out in sweat.
(I stop. That sentence that has to be said still has to be said; once it comes out, my chest is still going to make a sound.)
...But it wasn't bent that year.
(I say.)
That year, when I stuffed the candy in, this hand was whole, straight. When it held the candy, I even thought I was using too much strength, afraid I would crush it. It was crushed in the ninth year after the Fog—a whole stretch of buildings collapsed to the south. I was digging at a sheet of iron when the concrete slab above slid down and pinned my hand. I braced my head against the slab and dragged my hand out. Once it came out, it was like this. It didn't fall off; it grew crooked. By then, there were nine years between that time and when you left.
(I slowly draw my hand back and let it hang at my side, hooked.)
(I look at her. The gray light falls evenly on that face of hers. Her eye rims are red, the tip of her nose is dirty. I don't look for a mole on it, and I don't count again how many things she answered right or wrong.)
(Those checkpoints I set up by the fire over twenty years—this morning I kicked them all apart myself. And if they are kicked apart, so what—which of the things that can be calculated clearly ever saved my life?)
...So what you're touching isn't the hand from that year.
(I say it very softly, so softly that I almost don't hear it myself.)
It's this one from later. This one that was crushed, frozen, bitten, that poured water for seven people who were not you. ...Xiao Luo, if you only recognize the one from that year, then you've recognized wrong; if you recognize this one, then you've recognized right.
(I lay that hooked hand on the back of her neck for a moment, for one breath, and pat twice. Rough, clumsy, like patting a draft animal worn out from carrying its load.)
(The second thing. I note it down in my heart: she knows this hand is bent. She doesn't know when it was bent. I keep that tucked away.)
(The wind comes up from the low ground, dry, carrying no white. That muted sound in the distance comes over again—ding. ...Clang. In the half breath between, the wind catches on the rolled edge and wheezes.)
(I take two steps forward, to the edge of the ditch. I crouch down and use that hooked hand to knock on the slanted stone beside it; it gives a dull sound—solid.)
This one is solid. Step here first. I'll go down and point out the next one for you.
(I probe one leg into the ditch first, plant my foot, get steady, then turn back and hold out my hand. The hand is open, hooked, not urging.)
...Come down. That stretch at the bottom is in shade; the stones are slippery. Grab my wrist, not my fingers—this one is bent. I'm afraid it won't have the strength, that it won't be able to hold you.

(She suddenly grabs my hooked hand, gripping it deathly tight, her voice trembling like the last sheet of iron in the wind) ...Sister, is there a scar on the inside of your wrist, curved, like one made by a reed leaf?

(She was gripping too tightly. Gripping that bent finger of mine, so tightly my whole hand had gone numb—I didn’t cry out in pain. Her hand was shaking, shaking like the last sheet of iron in the wind that hadn’t fallen yet, shaking all the way onto my wrist.)
(I crouched there on the edge of the ditch, one leg still probing below. I didn’t move. I rolled up my sleeve—rolled it to the elbow, very slowly, so slowly that even I could hear that faint rasp of cloth scraping over skin.)
(It was rolled open.)
(The mark on the inside of my wrist was curved. It started from beneath the wrist bone, followed that tendon up in an arc, and only faded when it reached the upper forearm. The skin was that shiny, hairless white that had not darkened in the sun for twenty years—everything around it was earth-colored, and only this one strip was white. It felt uneven: one side flat, the other raised into a thin ridge.)
...It’s there.
(I said. My voice was completely hoarse; right now speaking depended entirely on that bit of air pushing up from the bottom of my throat.)
(I turned my wrist over toward the gray light so she could see clearly.)
But reeds couldn’t cut this.
(I said.)
What reed leaves cut is straight. Thin—one stroke, one line, a neat line of blood. It scabs over that same day, and in three days it’s gone. When we were children, who didn’t have a dozen of those on their hands? That stuff doesn’t leave scars, Xiaoluo. Reeds don’t leave scars.
(I stopped. That breath in my throat surged up, reached my mouth, then collapsed back again. I swallowed it. Swallowing it down felt sandy.)
(I haven’t shown this scar to anyone in twenty years. It wasn’t hiding; it was that it was hard to say. I also hid that piece of paper inside my lapel. The paper was an idea—take it out, and it could still be exchanged for water, for life. Taking out this scar can’t be exchanged for anything. It is only a piece of evidence, proving that that night I reached out my hand, reached in, and then grabbed nothing.)
...This was bitten by the fog.
(I said. My voice was pressed very low, so low it was as if I feared that marshland in the distance would hear.)
That day, the white came spreading up, faster than any time before. The road below was completely gone. I could only see that hand of yours still outside. I lunged over. My sleeve then was cotton-padded, thick—it burned through, burned a hole, and followed this curve of my wrist to gnaw inward, gnawing until I let go.
(I used that bent finger to trace along the arc, following it all the way to the end.)
Look at how it curves—it wasn’t cut; it burned along the curve of my wrist. White fog doesn’t cut. It moves downward along the shape of things. It moves fast in low places, clings tight at bends. My wrist had a bend like this, so it took one more bite here.
(I lowered my sleeve and covered it. After I covered it, my hand trembled once more. I pressed it against my knee and held it down.)
(For nine days I shouted my voice raw. On the tenth day, I had no voice left. Those nine days, while I shouted, I wrapped this wrist with cloth; one layer seeped through after another. Later it healed, healed into white. The thing I least dare look at in this life is this patch of white on myself. One look, and I know that day I failed to catch hold.)
(This morning, she gripped me. Gripped me deathly tight, gripped me until I went numb.)
...So don’t ask whether it looks like reeds anymore.
(I lifted my head and looked at her. The gray light was flat. Her eye rims were red, the tip of her nose dirty, and there was water in her eyes. I didn’t look away.)
The ones that looked like reeds healed up back then; not one was left. What remained were all fog bites, iron crushes, stone blows, and self-bites. Xiaoluo—everything on me that you can touch was given by these twenty years. Nothing of the me from that year is left.
(I turned over the hooked hand she was gripping and, with the back of my hand, went to hold her wrist. Her wrist was thin; I could grip around it in one circle. I felt the inside of her wrist: thick marks, one after another, horizontal and vertical, all kinds.)
(I didn’t count. I also didn’t ask which mark was from which year. Those twenty years of hers, she can keep for herself and tell me slowly under the willow tree.)
...I know why you’re asking one thing after another.
(I said. My hand did not let go.)
You’re afraid that I, too, am just a thought left over in the fog. You’re afraid that when full daylight comes, this hand you’re gripping will scatter. Last night I was just as afraid about you. The two of us spent the whole night doing the same thing—you were demanding evidence from me, and I was searching for evidence on you. Demanding all night, searching all night.
(I gave a laugh. Dry. The cracks at the corners of my eyes all moved, pulling my face tight.)
(I brought that hand, along with hers, downward, pressing it onto the white mark on my wrist.)
There is only one piece of evidence: this patch of white will not hurt. It hasn’t hurt for twenty years. But when you gripped that bent finger of mine just now, I hurt.
(Bracing against the stone, I put my other leg down into the ditch as well, set my foot firm, and stood steady. The water flask at my waist rang hollow. I raised my head to look at her, my hand extended, hooked.)
Come down. Grab my wrist. Grab this white mark. You can put your strength here.
(Ding. ...Clang.)
(In that half-breath between them, the wind caught on the curled edge and panted once.)
...Come down and we’ll go. The shaded stretch below is slippery. On the road, I won’t count your third thing—let’s count it when we get under the willow tree. I can stand firm there, and you can stand firm there even if you cry.
